nameStory: Pylaisiadelpha moss gets its tongue-twisting scientific name from the Greek botanist Pylaisios, with 'adelpha' meaning 'sister' or 'related to.' The species name 'tenuirostris' means 'thin-beaked,' referring to the slender shape of its spore capsules. While it lacks a widely-used common name, some botanists simply call it 'slender-beaked feather moss.'
description: Pylaisiadelpha moss is a delicate feathery moss that forms thin, sprawling mats on tree bark and occasionally rocks. Its tiny branches create an intricate, lace-like pattern that's quite beautiful when you look closely. Individual plants are small, typically only growing a few centimeters long, but they can spread to cover substantial patches of bark. This moss has a glossy, almost silky appearance when dry and becomes more vibrant green when moist.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms thin, feathery mats that spread horizontally across bark surfaces, creating delicate branching patterns that feel almost paper-thin to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, overlapping leaves that lie flat against the stem, giving branches a flattened, scale-like appearance visible with a hand lens

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Slender, elongated capsules on thin stalks that curve gracefully like tiny shepherd's crooks when mature

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Glossy yellow-green to golden-brown when dry, becoming brighter emerald green when wet, with a subtle sheen

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on smooth bark of deciduous trees, particularly maples and birches, rarely found on rough bark or other surfaces

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels remarkably smooth and silky when you gently run your finger across it, quite different from the rougher texture of cushion mosses

habitat: Look for this moss on the smooth bark of deciduous trees in moist woodlands throughout New England, particularly on maples, birches, and occasionally oaks. It prefers the protected north sides of trees in mature forests where humidity stays relatively high. You'll rarely find it in dry, exposed areas or on very rough bark.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green as spring moisture returns, with new growth appearing as bright green tips on existing mats.
seasonality.summer: May look somewhat dry and golden during hot spells but quickly greens up after rain showers.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most visible as deciduous canopy opens up, allowing more light to reach the moss-covered bark.
seasonality.winter: Remains present but often appears more golden-brown and compressed, though it stays alive under snow and ice.

funFact: This moss is so rare in New England that it's been documented only once in the entire region, making any sighting a genuine botanical treasure hunt success story!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other feathery bark mosses, but Pylaisiadelpha's distinctively flattened, scale-like leaves and preference for very smooth bark help distinguish it. Remember: if the bark is rough or the moss feels fluffy rather than silky-smooth, you're probably looking at a different species.
contextualKnowledge: Being part of the Sematophyllaceae family, this moss represents a group that's more common in tropical regions, making its presence in New England quite remarkable from a biogeographical perspective.
compareHints: Since this is the only Pylaisiadelpha species in New England, compare it with other members of the Sematophyllaceae family, which tend to be glossy, feathery mosses. Pylaisiadelpha differs by having more flattened branching patterns and showing a stronger preference for very smooth bark surfaces. Its leaves also lie flatter against the stem than most related species, creating that distinctive scale-like appearance.
